title: Quantum Key Distribution with Entanglement-Swapped Photons from a Quantum Emitter
authors: Michele B. Rota, Francesco Basso Basset, Alessandro Laneve, Francesco Salusti, Nicolas Claro-Rodriguez, Giuseppe Ronco, Mattia Beccaceci, Tobias M. Krieger, Quirin Buchinger, Saimon F. Covre da Silva, Sandra Stroj, Mariia Gumberidze, Vladyslav Usenko, Sven Höfling, Tobias Huber-Loyola, Mario A. Usuga Castaneda, Armando Rastelli, Klaus D. Jöns, Rinaldo Trotta
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is a fundamental functionality of quantum networks. Extending its range requires quantum repeaters, a technology still under development and not yet demonstrated in combination with quantum cryptographic protocols. Here, we address the elementary operation of a viable quantum repeater scheme by evaluating whether correlated photons distributed via entanglement swapping can support secret key distribution. We employ a state-of-the-art deterministic photon source based on a strain-tuned GaAs quantum dot embedded in a photonic cavity and implement a source-independent QKD protocol between two nodes using entanglement-swapped photons. We benchmark the system and present how high-resolution temporal post-selection can enable secure key exchange, with further rate improvements expected through realistic device and protocol optimizations. Due to its compatibility with a wide range of quantum memory platforms, our approach represents a significant step towards long-distance quantum-safe communication.
summary: This paper demonstrates a crucial step toward long-distance quantum communication by implementing a quantum repeater protocol using entanglement-swapped photons. They utilize a deterministic photon source based on a GaAs quantum dot embedded in a photonic cavity. The experiment successfully shows that secure key distribution can be achieved by carefully controlling the temporal post-selection during the entanglement swapping process.
main_problem: The primary goal is to extend the range of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) by implementing an elementary quantum repeater scheme using entanglement-swapped photons.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated secure key exchange using entanglement-swapped photons generated from a quantum dot source, achieving a maximum positive asymptotic secure key fraction (SKF) of 9.8% under optimized temporal post-selection.
method: The protocol involves generating two pairs of entangled photons, performing a Bell State Measurement (BSM) on the intermediate photons, and then using the remaining photons for an entanglement-based QKD protocol (asymmetrical Ekert variation).
model_or_system: The system utilizes a state-of-the-art deterministic photon source: a strain-tuned GaAs quantum dot embedded in a photonic cavity and integrated on a piezoelectric substrate. This source generates strongly polarization-entangled photon pairs via the biexciton-exciton cascade.
key_observables: Fidelity of the emitted state (0.94(1)), HOM visibility (improved to 0.79(2)), Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER), Bell parameter (S), and the Secure Key Fraction (SKF).
important_parameters: The performance is highly dependent on the BSM coincidence temporal window, with optimal results found at short time delays (e.g., 30 ps).
main_assumptions: The security analysis assumes Alice and Bob control their measuring apparatuses, and the protocol relies on temporal post-selection rather than entanglement distillation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the protocol scheme involving entanglement swapping (Fig. 1), the entanglement swapping performance vs. BSM coincidence time window (Fig. 2), and the QKD setup detailing source, BSM, and measurement stations (Fig. 3).
paper_structure: The paper details the theoretical framework for quantum repeaters, describes the experimental setup using QD sources, presents measurements of entanglement swapping fidelity and QKD parameters (QBER, S) as a function of the BSM coincidence window, and concludes with the calculation of the secure key rate.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the physical realization of quantum networks by integrating solid-state quantum emitters (QDs) into a functional quantum repeater architecture for QKD, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems research.
